title: Trump’s Men in the Middle East
gist: Chatham House's Renad Mansour documents an explicit Trump administration doctrine, driven by envoy Tom Barrack: back individual strongmen who centralize state power in Iraq, Syria and Lebanon, and expect them to roll back Iran and open their economies to American firms. Washington's hardest lever is financial — Iraq's oil revenues sit in a US Federal Reserve account and a Treasury freeze forced Baghdad to replace Maliki with banker Ali al-Zaidi — but Mansour argues centralization is failing everywhere: IRGC officers are rebuilding Hezbollah, Israel is paying 3,000 Druze militia salaries in Syria, and Sharaa is already refusing Washington's demands.

themes.theme: The strongman doctrine as stated policy

insights.claim: The emerging US approach to the Levant, cultivated above all by Trump envoy Tom Barrack, is to identify leaders who can centralize state power, back them personally, and count on them to push back against Iranian influence and open their economies to American business.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The doctrine explains which Middle East leaders will receive US commercial and diplomatic backing — a screen for where American firms get preferential access.
insights.locator: The warmth is not incidental.

insights.claim: Where recent US administrations spoke of power sharing and negotiated political settlements in Middle East governance, the Trump administration is openly wagering on strongmen and judging partners not by how they govern but by what they can deliver.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Removes governance conditionality from US engagement, lowering political-risk friction for deals but raising the odds of abrupt reversals when a patron falls.
insights.quote: the measure of a partner is not how he governs but what he can deliver
insights.locator: For Trump, the appeal of these leaders

insights.claim: Trump publicly signaled personal investment in Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the Oval Office in mid-July 2026, praising his 'tremendous chemistry' and twice saying Zaidi would be there 'for a long time' while calling Iraq's wealth 'not only potential.'
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: A presidential guarantee of tenure for an unelected compromise premier — read it as a green light for US commercial entry into Iraqi oil and reconstruction.
insights.locator: Standing beside Iraq’s new prime minister

insights.claim: Trump hosted Lebanese President Joseph Aoun in July 2026, the first Lebanese head of state invited to the White House in more than 15 years, folding him into the same strongman project.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: A 15-year diplomatic reopening tied to disarmament expectations — marks Lebanon as newly eligible for US-backed reconstruction capital.
insights.locator: Finally, this week, Trump hosted Lebanese President Joseph Aoun

insights.claim: Trump's appeal in these leaders is a single interlocutor who commands the state, its security forces and its economy — worth more to Washington than a shaky coalition because he can sign oil and reconstruction deals with American firms and maintain stability without US troops or attention.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: US Middle East policy is now explicitly deal-oriented and troop-light: expect commercial announcements to substitute for security guarantees.
insights.locator: For Trump, the appeal of these leaders lies in their promise

themes.theme: Iraq: Fed-account leverage and a manufactured premier

insights.claim: Because Iraq's oil revenues sit in an account at the US Federal Reserve and are flown to Baghdad as cash shipments, Washington controls Iraq's access to its own money — and a Treasury freeze of that lifeline generated significant political pressure.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The single most powerful and underappreciated US lever in the region: Iraqi sovereign liquidity is a Washington policy instrument, a live risk for Iraqi debt and contracts.
insights.locator: In Iraq, the search for Washington’s man began with a veto.

insights.claim: After Iraq's November 2025 elections the ruling Shiite Coordination Framework deadlocked for months before nominating former Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki in late January 2026, and Trump publicly vetoed the candidacy as too close to Tehran.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Direct US veto power over Iraqi premiership selection — Iraqi political outcomes are partly a function of Washington preference, not domestic arithmetic.
insights.locator: After the November 2025 elections

insights.claim: Ali al-Zaidi was a 40-year-old banker with no political base and no government experience when nominated, and his weakness was precisely his appeal — Baghdad's elites saw a compromise candidate who would implement their policy while Washington found its man.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: A premier with no independent base cannot enforce the reforms both sponsors expect — structural reason to discount Iraqi disarmament and anti-corruption commitments.
insights.locator: Iraq’s political class got the message

insights.claim: Trump claimed Zaidi 'won the election very soundly' when in fact Zaidi was never even a candidate, an inaccuracy Mansour highlights as revealing how little the administration's narrative tracks Iraqi political reality.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Official US framing of regional partners is unreliable as an information source; verify legitimacy claims independently before pricing stability.
insights.quote: Trump would later claim that Zaidi “won the election very soundly.” He did not. In fact, he was never even a candidate.
insights.locator: Trump would later claim that Zaidi

insights.claim: Zaidi committed to disarm and integrate the Popular Mobilization Forces including Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba, and to launch an anti-corruption drive sold to Americans as part of the same project.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: These are the specific deliverables against which US support for Baghdad will be judged — and their failure is the trigger for renewed financial pressure.
insights.locator: But Zaidi played the role assigned to him

insights.claim: Iraq's political system was deliberately fragmented after Saddam Hussein so that no single actor can dominate, meaning the centralization Washington wants runs against the system's design rather than merely against vested interests.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Institutional design, not personnel, is the constraint — no Iraqi premier can deliver the centralization Washington's doctrine assumes.
insights.locator: After the experience of Saddam

insights.claim: Zaidi's disarmament push will likely reproduce past failures by granting armed groups state salaries and patronage while their loyalties stay with their own commanders rather than the central government.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Expect nominal integration announcements with no change in command loyalty — do not treat disarmament headlines as de-risking events.
insights.locator: Zaidi’s disarmament push will likely reproduce

insights.claim: Pro-government Iraqi groups such as the Sadrists and Asaib Ahl al-Haq have announced weapons-inventory committees while the more Iran-aligned Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba have refused and signaled they will turn on the Iraqi state itself if pushed too far.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: A named split in the militia landscape identifies which actors pose escalation risk to US interests and Iraqi state functions.
insights.locator: While pro-government groups, such as the Sadrists

insights.claim: The war with Iran has reversed the axis of resistance's recent decentralization: the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps has taken a more active and commanding role in Iraq, directing resistance factions and using the country as a launching pad for Tehran's regional strategy.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The war has made Iranian proxy control tighter, not looser — a second-order effect that inverts the stated US objective.
insights.locator: And where the “axis of resistance” had grown more decentralized

insights.claim: Many in the Iraqi government genuinely want to rein in militias because armed groups outside the chain of command undermine sovereignty and risk dragging Iraq into unwanted wars — but wanting sovereignty and being able to enforce it are different things, particularly on Washington's timeline.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Capacity, not intent, is the binding constraint; US deadlines will produce visible non-compliance rather than reform.
insights.quote: But wanting sovereignty and being able to enforce it are different things.
insights.locator: Many in the Iraqi government want to rein in the militias

insights.claim: The killing of an Iraqi government intelligence officer in March 2026, attributed by some officials to resistance groups, highlights the ongoing danger from militias to the state itself.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence that militia-state conflict is already kinetic, not hypothetical — raising internal security risk in Iraq.
insights.locator: The killing of a government intelligence officer in March

insights.claim: Barrack has turned against Washington's earlier commitment to Iraqi pluralism, now describing the Baghdad-Erbil federal model — once treated as a pillar of the new Iraq — not as moderation but as 'Balkanization.'
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: US backing for Kurdish autonomy is weakening — direct risk to Kurdistan Region energy contracts and revenue-sharing arrangements.
insights.locator: And here too, Barrack has turned against Washington’s commitment

themes.theme: Syria: template that is already resisting

insights.claim: Syria has become the template for the strongman doctrine: Trump announced in Riyadh in May 2025 he would end Assad-era sanctions, Washington later removed terrorist designations on Ahmed al-Sharaa himself, and Sharaa's image transformed from a man with a $10 million bounty on his head to a White House guest.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The full sanctions-and-designation reversal defines how fast US legal status can change for a partner leader — and how fast it could reverse.
insights.locator: Syria has become the template.

insights.claim: Sharaa's early pitch to Washington reportedly included a proposal for a Trump Tower in Damascus, detente with Israel, and cooperation enabling US access to Syria's oil and gas.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Names the commercial currency of access under this administration — branded real estate and hydrocarbon concessions as diplomatic instruments.
insights.locator: Sharaa knows his audience

insights.claim: Barrack has pushed for a centralized Syrian state, declaring 'one nation, one people, one army, one Syria' and that 'federalism does not work' in the region — a break from post-Assad thinking that stability required guaranteeing Kurds, Druze and Alawites a share of power and autonomy.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Explicit abandonment of minority power-sharing raises the probability of communal conflict in Syria — a security-premium factor for reconstruction investment.
insights.quote: We all need to reconcile and come to this conclusion: one nation, one people, one army, one Syria,
insights.locator: Barrack, who works closely with Damascus

insights.claim: Barrack said of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces, Washington's own partner against the Islamic State, that 'we don't owe them the ability to have their own independent government within a government' and announced in January that their political role had 'largely expired.'
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: US abandonment of the SDF is now explicit policy language — a signal for northeast Syria security and any energy or aid operations there.
insights.quote: We don’t owe them the ability to have their own independent government within a government,
insights.locator: “We don’t owe them the ability

insights.claim: Sharaa is using US backing to consolidate his own rule rather than subordinating himself to US designs: he objected to Trump's floated idea of Syria taking on Hezbollah in Lebanon and told Barrack that compromising on the Golan would mean the end of his rule.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The strongman is already defecting from the bargain — expect US-Syria friction and unmet expectations on Israel normalization.
insights.quote: the basic elements of trust are simply not there.
insights.locator: More fundamentally, Sharaa is unlikely to simply align

insights.claim: July 2025 clashes in Syria's Druze-majority Suwayda province killed hundreds; when Sharaa sent forces in, local leaders accused them of widespread abuses and Israel — casting itself as the Druze's protector — bombed Syrian government troops.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that Syrian centralization attempts trigger Israeli military intervention — a recurring escalation channel independent of US policy.
insights.locator: Syria is different because Sharaa has gone furthest

insights.claim: Israel has been paying the salaries of some 3,000 Druze militia fighters in Syria and supplying them with weapons, actively unifying the very factions Sharaa is meant to absorb into the state.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: A US ally is directly funding fragmentation of the state Washington is trying to centralize — the doctrine's internal contradiction, quantified.
insights.locator: Since then, Israel has been paying the salaries

insights.claim: Israel's campaign shattered Hezbollah's military capabilities and undermined its long-held veto over Lebanese politics, letting a government of independent technocrats more critical of Hezbollah's state-within-a-state step into the vacuum.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Explains the window Washington is trying to exploit in Lebanon — and why its durability depends on Hezbollah's rebuild pace.
insights.locator: In Lebanon, Israel’s campaign against Hezbollah

insights.claim: Joseph Aoun was elected Lebanese president in January 2025 after commanding the Lebanese Armed Forces, and in August 2025 his government committed to disarming all groups with heavy weapons including Hezbollah, tasking the army with establishing a weapons monopoly by year-end.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: A dated, verifiable commitment whose visible failure is the trigger for renewed US pressure or Israeli action on Lebanon.
insights.locator: One figure in particular caught the Trump administration’s eye

insights.claim: Hezbollah has refused disarmament despite massive setbacks, and Iran's IRGC officers have arrived in Lebanon to oversee rebuilding of Hezbollah's military infrastructure, filling gaps left by the group's decapitated leadership.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Direct IRGC operational involvement means Hezbollah's degradation is temporary — argue against pricing a durable Lebanese security improvement.
insights.locator: When it comes to Hezbollah specifically

insights.claim: Israel has continued near-daily attacks on Lebanon despite the November 2024 cease-fire and still occupies multiple positions in the south, while a war that killed more than 4,000 people and displaced 1.2 million fell mainly on Lebanon's Shiites, who see a government unable to protect or represent them.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Ongoing occupation and strikes strengthen Hezbollah's resistance narrative, making the disarmament objective self-defeating.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the conditions on the ground undercut Aoun.

insights.claim: Mansour argues that moving aggressively against Hezbollah while Israel bombs and occupies Lebanon would fracture rather than extend state authority, and that negotiating with an occupying power only strengthens Hezbollah's rhetoric of resistance — the Lebanese army has itself acknowledged limited disarmament capability.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The US roadmap is structurally self-defeating in Lebanon; civil-conflict risk rises with the pace of pressure.
insights.locator: The army has itself acknowledged its limited capabilities

insights.claim: When Barrack warned that Lebanon would cease to exist as a state if it failed to move on disarmament, Aoun publicly dismissed the remarks and insisted the process would proceed at the army's pace, not Washington's — the doctrine's client openly refusing its timeline.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Public defiance by a hand-picked partner is the clearest evidence the strongman bet is not producing compliance.
insights.locator: The strains are already showing

insights.claim: Lebanon's confessional system was built to prevent central political dominance and dispersed power so thoroughly that when the balance collapsed the result was 15 years of civil war — making it the least suitable of the three states for the centralization doctrine.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Ranks Lebanon as the highest-risk of the three bets; civil-war recurrence is the tail scenario to hedge.
insights.locator: Finally, Lebanon is in a different and more challenging category.

themes.theme: Historical base rate: strongmen deliver fragility

insights.claim: The strongman doctrine has been tried before in these very countries and failed: Saddam Hussein centralized Iraq so completely that his rule produced ruinous wars, and the Assads held Syria together for five decades through a coercive apparatus that hollowed out institutions and ultimately drove Syrians to revolt.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The historical base rate is that centralization produces delayed catastrophic instability, not durable stability — a long-horizon risk for any regional exposure.
insights.locator: But there is every reason to think that it will prove naïve.

insights.claim: Mansour's conclusion is that Trump's transactional approach prioritizes quick visible wins over long-term settlements in a region whose entrenched political dynamics are not susceptible to quick wins, making the gamble more likely to reignite conflict and weaken US interests than to produce lasting political change.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: The central bearish call: expect renewed Middle East conflict rather than consolidation, with US-aligned partners bearing the costs.
insights.locator: Trump’s approach is fundamentally transactional

insights.claim: In this form of personalized diplomacy relationships substitute for institutions, so US regional policy carries concentrated single-person risk in each of Iraq, Syria and Lebanon.
insights.speaker: Renad Mansour
insights.so_what: Each partner's removal or death would reset US position from scratch — a discontinuity risk to price into regional commercial commitments.
insights.quote: In this form of personalized diplomacy, where relationships substitute for institutions
insights.locator: It also means signing oil and reconstruction deals
